draft.title: The Great Terror
card: The Great Terror was a wave of purges, or removals of suspected enemies, in the Soviet Union from 1936 to 1938. It was run by the secret police, the NKVD.
Many victims were accused of plotting against the state or spying for foreign powers. Confessions were often forced by pressure and torture.
Hundreds of thousands were executed. Many more were sent to Gulag labour camps, where they did hard labour in harsh conditions.
The targets included senior party leaders and army officers, as well as ordinary citizens. Even loyal members could be accused, so fear spread through society.
draft.remember: The Terror turned on loyal members of the party and army as well as ordinary people, and it spread fear.

a.q: Which description best fits the Great Terror of 1936 to 1938?
opts: A purge that hit party leaders, officers and ordinary people
A purge aimed only at peasants who resisted collective farms
A purge carried out by the army against the secret police
A purge that ended with every Gulag prisoner set free
a.why: The Terror struck senior party members and army officers as well as ordinary citizens. It was not limited to peasants, because accusations of plotting or spying could fall on almost anyone, and the secret police ran it.
a.clue: Think about who could be accused, and who ran the purges.

b.q: In 1937 a loyal Soviet army officer is arrested and confesses to spying for a foreign power. Which explanation fits the Great Terror best?
opts: Confessions were often forced, and loyal people could be accused
Only proven traitors were arrested, so the confession was true
Officers were safe because the army was outside the purges
Arrests were rare, as most victims were quietly left alone
b.why: During the Terror, confessions were often forced by pressure and torture, and even loyal members could be accused. The idea that only proven traitors were arrested is tempting, but the charges were often false and the targets wide.
b.clue: Ask how confessions were obtained, and whether loyalty gave protection.
